name: Linear Regression
tagline: The starting point of machine learning: finding the best-fit hyperplane.
introduction: Linear Regression is the fundamental supervised algorithm for regression tasks. It models the relationship between a continuous dependent target variable y and one or more independent explanatory features X by fitting a linear equation. The algorithm seeks coefficients that minimize the sum of squared differences between actual and predicted values.
why_used: Unmatched simplicity, transparency, and computational speed.
Directly inspectable coefficients show the precise marginal effect of each input variable.
Serves as the analytical baseline for all quantitative predictive modeling.
Exact analytical closed-form solution (Normal Equation) exists for moderately sized data.
how_it_works:
1. Hypothesize a linear relationship: y = w_0 + w_1*x_1 + w_2*x_2 + ... + w_n*x_n + epsilon.
2. Measure prediction errors (residuals) e_i = y_i - y_hat_i.
3. Define the objective function as the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS).
4. Find the optimal weights (w) that minimize RSS using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) closed-form matrix algebra or iterative Gradient Descent.
mathematical_intuition: Geometrically, in 2D space, linear regression fits the straight line y = mx + c that minimizes the vertical squared distances from all data points to the line. In n dimensions, it fits an (n-1)-dimensional hyperplane.

important_formulas.name: Linear Hypothesis
important_formulas.description: Predicted target is a linear weighted sum of feature inputs plus an intercept bias term.

important_formulas.name: Ordinary Least Squares (RSS Objective)
important_formulas.description: Sum of squared residual errors minimized by the OLS estimator.

important_formulas.name: Normal Equation (Closed-form Solution)
important_formulas.description: Exact optimal weight vector, assuming (X^T * X) is invertible (non-singular).

important_formulas.name: Coefficient of Determination (R² Score)
important_formulas.description: Proportion of target variance explained by the model features (1.0 = perfect fit, 0.0 = baseline mean prediction).

step_by_step_example.scenario: Predicting apartment rent (y, in thousands) based on square footage (x, in hundreds).
step_by_step_example.prediction: For a 1200 sq ft apartment (x=12): Rent = 2.5 * 12 = 30 ($3,000).

advantages: Completely transparent: each coefficient directly quantifies feature impact.
Extremely fast to compute and requires negligible memory.
Deterministic closed-form solution exists without need for hyperparameter tuning.
Can easily incorporate regularization (Ridge L2, Lasso L1) to prevent overfitting.
disadvantages: Strong assumption: assumes strictly linear additive relationships between inputs and target.
Highly sensitive to outliers: squaring errors places immense penalty on extreme values, skewing the line.
Susceptible to multicollinearity (correlated features create unstable, erratic coefficients).
Prone to high bias (underfitting) when true relationships are non-linear or curved.
when_to_use: When relationships between variables are genuinely linear or approximately linear.
When you need to explain how much the target increases per unit increase of a feature.
As the standard quantitative benchmark before testing non-linear algorithms.
when_to_avoid: When relationships exhibit non-linear thresholds, saturation curves, or complex interactions.
When data contains uncleaned extreme anomalies/outliers.

comparison_with_related.difference: Linear Regression fits a smooth global continuous plane; Decision Tree Regressors partition space into piecewise flat step regions.
Linear Regression has high bias and cannot learn curves without polynomial features; Random Forests naturally capture non-linear surfaces by averaging trees.

practical_example: Predicting house prices or quarterly business revenue based on historical marketing spend and square footage.
